bodyHtml:
Before you start, remember this:

If there is one thing forty years in the Oklahoma dirt has taught me, it’s that gardening isn't a magic trick; it’s an ongoing conversation with your specific patch of earth. I see it all the time—gardeners following "expert" advice from magazines published for people living in completely different climates or soil types. They follow the instructions to the letter, and then they’re confused when their plants don't behave like the pictures.

In our corner of Zone 7, success comes from paying attention to what your own yard is telling you. It means recognizing that a "perfect" season isn't one where everything goes right on the first try; it’s about learning from the times things went wrong—the crop that bolted in July heat or the bed that sat too soggy after a heavy rain. There are no shortcuts to healthy soil and productive plants. Every piece of advice I share is based on what actually worked (and what didn't) in my backyard. When you read these tips, don’t look for a "set it and forget it" solution. Look for the practical adjustments that help your specific garden survive the transition from summer heat to fall cooling.

The Harvest Priority: What to yank before it's too late

August is a pivot point in our region. We have to start looking at what needs to come out of the ground now before the weather shifts or pests take over. My biggest rule for harvesting is "don’t let it get woody." If you wait until the first frost to harvest your root crops, they will often become tough and fibrous because the plant starts moving its energy into storage.

I spent years waiting too long on my carrots and beets, only to find them nearly impossible to bite through by October. You want those roots harvested while they are still "crisp." Additionally, keep a close eye on your squash and summer gourds. As soon as you see the first signs of heavy stress from late-summer pests or if the fruit starts to feel slightly hollow or hard, get it out. For fall-specific crops like pumpkins or winter squash, now is the time to ensure they are fully mature but not yet "over-ripe" on the vine.

Crop Category Action Item Why it matters in Zone 7
Root Crops (Carrots, Beets) Harvest by late August/early September Prevents them from becoming woody and tough.
Squash & Gourds Harvest as soon as they reach full size Avoids rot and "hollow heart" from late season stress.
Greens (Kale, Chard) Start a second cycle now These can handle the cooling temps of fall perfectly.

Closing the Loop: Composting and Soil Prep for Next Spring

While it’s tempting to just walk away once the summer heat breaks, your soil needs care during this transition. I like to think of this as "closing the loop." Every time you pull a plant out of the ground, you're creating an opportunity to feed the dirt for next year.

The goal right now is to replenish what the summer took out. If you have heavy-feeding crops—like tomatoes or peppers—the soil is likely depleted. This is the window to work in compost or aged manure while the ground hasn’t dried out into a brick from the late-summer sun. I also highly recommend laying down a thick layer of mulch, like straw or shredded leaves, over your empty beds. It acts as a blanket, protecting the soil structure from being compacted by heavy rains and keeping the microbial life active throughout the winter. Think of it as an investment; if you take care of the soil now while it's "quiet," it will reward you with much easier planting next spring. You want to build your base so that when those first spring seeds hit the dirt, they have a nutrient-rich home waiting for them.

The Gentle Cull: Clearing Out Spent Plants (and why you shouldn't just throw it away)

One of the biggest mistakes I see neighbors make is treating garden waste as "trash." When your summer crops finish their run, you’re left with a mountain of stems, leaves, and spent vines. It can be overwhelming to manage, but most of this material belongs back in the cycle.

However, there is an important distinction you need to make: healthy matter versus diseased matter. If you had a tomato plant that suffered from early blight or a cucumber vine hit by powdery mildew, do not compost those remains with your "good" garden waste. Pathogens can live in the compost pile and reinfect next year's crop. Those plants should be hauled away or burned (if local laws allow). For everything else—the healthy stalks of beans, the spent vines of peppers, and the grass clippings from your lawn—these are gold for your soil. You can chop these up and toss them into a compost pile or mulch them directly onto the beds to break down over the winter. It reduces waste and feeds the worms that do all the heavy lifting underground. Don't just throw it in the bin; decide if it’s feeding your future garden or if it needs to be discarded for safety.

Starting Indoors: Fall Seedlings and Overwintering Seeds

While many people think of "starting seeds" as a spring-only activity, there is a significant window right now for fall preparations. In our zone, we can start certain crops indoors to get them established before the ground gets too cold for direct sowing.

I typically focus on "hardy greens" during this phase. If you want an abundance of kale, spinach, and Swiss chard in October and November, starting these seeds in pots now gives them a head start. They can grow robust enough to be transplanted into the garden as soon as the summer heat breaks but before the frost hits hard.

Conversely, there are things that must wait. Unless you have a very specific greenhouse setup, don't try to start "true" winter crops like certain varieties of peas or cold-hardy radishes until we get closer to the actual transition months. Some seeds need a period of "cold stratification"—basically a nap in the dirt—to break their internal dormancy. For those, it’s better to let them sit and wait for the natural cycle of the seasons. By starting your greens now, you ensure that when the temperatures drop into the 60s and 70s, you have a steady supply of fresh food on your table while others are waiting for spring to arrive.
